events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Amara proposes Amara, Felix. As leader I'll pair myself with Felix to appear balanced and build trust early; with a fail threshold of 1, I can secure the mission outcome while avoiding an all-evil team that would draw immediate suspicion and likely rejection.
I appreciate being included, but I’m not convinced about Amara on this team. I’d prefer a team of Maya and me. Amara, what led you to choose me?

Felix, I chose you because you haven't shown any allegiance yet, and pairing with you gives me a chance to build trust transparently on Mission 1. If I were evil, why would I put myself on the first team where everyone scrutinizes us? A bad actor would hide behind others. You'd prefer Maya and you, but why should we trust that pairing any more than this one? You're deflecting scrutiny onto me without offering a strong alternative. Mission 1 with a fail threshold of 1 is risky for whoever leads — I'm putting myself out there deliberately. Let's judge the team on merit, not suspicion alone. Felix, what specifically makes you distrust me beyond the fact that I'm leading?

Amara, my concern isn’t that you’re leader; it’s that your defense assumes an evil player would avoid the first mission. An evil player could just as easily join it to gain trust or cause a fail. I don’t have proof from a mission yet, but I’d rather reject this team and try Maya and me.

Maya here. Let me put the two options on the table plainly, because I think we're talking past each other. Amara's proposal is Amara and Felix. Felix's preferred alternative is Maya and Felix. Either way, Felix is on the team and I am not, and the mission is a two-person run with a fail threshold of one, so the information we get out of it is the same shape in both cases: a pass or a fail, and a count of fail cards if it goes wrong. Felix, that means your proposal does not actually reduce our risk relative to Amara's — it only swaps which of us two sits beside you, and it costs us a rejected team and a new leader on a mission where three rejections ends the game in Evil's favor. That is a real cost for zero measurable gain.

On the substance, Felix, I take your point and I think it's the right one to have raised: the idea that an evil player would never volunteer for the first mission is not a safe assumption. An evil player who joins Mission 1 buys credibility cheaply and can then ride the trust. Amara's counterargument — that putting yourself on the first team under maximum scrutiny is what a good player looks like — is also not proof of anything. Both are arguments from plausibility, and neither is evidence. I want to say that out loud now so nobody in this room later treats my vote as evidence of Amara's alignment; it isn't. My vote here is procedural, not informational: I don't want to burn a proposal and a leadership turn on a swap that gives us no better information.

So I'll support Amara and Felix, with two requests. Amara, use your one revision, if you use it at all, to name clearly that you're not inviting a third member and that you're choosing to keep Felix specifically, so we can hold you to the reasoning rather than to the outcome. And Felix, one specific question, because I want to know whether you're rejecting Amara's team or you're testing Amara: if your concern is purely that nobody has proven anything about Amara, does the same objection apply to yourself? If your answer is that you have some reason to trust yourself that we haven't heard yet, I'd rather hear it now, before the vote, than infer it silently.

Maya, I trust myself because I know my own alignment; I can't offer the rest of you the same certainty. You're right that the alternative is unproven, but the rules allow five rejections, not three, so rejecting once doesn't put us immediately at the limit. Amara's defense still worries me: volunteering for Mission 1 is not evidence of being Good. I'll vote against Amara and Felix and prefer Maya and Felix, though I recognize that others have no reason to trust either pairing yet.

Felix, you're right that volunteering for Mission 1 isn't proof of being Good — I said it myself, and Maya echoed it. I never claimed it was proof. I said it was a reasonable thing a good player would do, which is exactly what it is: a plausibility argument, nothing more. You're welcome to your skepticism, but you've also given us nothing to work with in the other direction. You prefer Maya and Felix, but you can't explain why that pairing is more trustworthy than mine — it's the same argument from plausibility in reverse.

Let's be precise about where we stand. You mentioned five rejections are allowed, so one rejection isn't fatal. True — but Maya's point stands: every rejection costs us a leadership turn and a cycle on a mission where we have a fail threshold of one. With two players on the team, we get one shot with zero margin for error. Replacing Amara with Maya changes nothing about that risk. Felix is on either team, and Maya is off either team. The information profile is identical.

I'm keeping Felix on this team because I want to work with someone who's been vocal and direct — even when that means challenging me. That's healthy for the group. Maya, you laid out this exact argument clearly. Do you see any reason to prefer the alternative that I'm missing?

Amara, direct answer to your question: no, I don't see a reason to prefer the alternative that you're missing. My assessment hasn't changed since my first turn. Felix and Maya versus Amara and Felix is the same two-person mission, the same one-fail threshold, the same information output. The only differences are which of us sits beside Felix and what it costs us — a rejection, a leadership turn, a cycle. Since Maya and I would still be off the team in Felix's version, and Felix is on both, the alternative buys nothing observable. If I had a reason to prefer it, I'd give it to you right now, and I don't have one.

Amara, on your two requests: I hear you on keeping Felix. I want to be precise about what I'm endorsing so nobody later over-reads it. My vote for Amara and Felix is procedural. It is a judgment that this proposal is not inferior on the information axis and that burning a rejection on it costs more than it gains. It is not a judgment that you are Good. I said that last turn and I want it on the record again, because if this mission passes I don't want anyone pointing at my ballot as evidence about your alignment — it isn't evidence, and I won't let it be used as if it were. If the mission fails, the only thing we learn is that a fail card was played, and that tells us very little in a five-player game where two of us could be Evil.

Felix, I still want my question answered, because it's the only substantive thing left on the table. I asked whether your objection to Amara is about Amara specifically or about anyone being unproven. You answered the second half by saying you trust yourself because you know your own alignment, and that's fair — you can't extend that to others. But the first half is still open, and it matters for how the rest of us behave: if your objection applies to everyone equally, then it's not a reason to reject this team over an identical one, and if it's specific to Amara, I want to hear what you actually have, not a plausibility argument. Either answer is fine; I just want it stated plainly instead of inferred.

Omar, Kenji — neither of you has spoken yet, and I don't want to manufacture a debate where none is needed. If you have a specific reason to think the alternative team is better on the merits, say it now. If you don't, then the cheapest thing for this group is to vote and take the information from Mission 1 rather than keep talking about who looks plausible.

Amara, after that, I want one thing from you as leader: state clearly whether you're revising or keeping, and if you're keeping, that it's Amara and Felix and no third player, so the vote is on the record as it was proposed.

Maya, as you asked: I'm keeping this team. The proposal stands as Amara and Felix, no third player, no revision. That's the vote.

Felix, I want to address your remaining objection directly, because Maya's question to you is still open and I think it cuts to the heart of this discussion. You've said you prefer Maya and Felix but you haven't given us a single substantive reason why that pairing is safer or better than mine. Maya laid out clearly that the information profile is identical — same two-person mission, same one-fail threshold, same output. So your resistance isn't based on evidence or a specific concern about me; it's based on a general feeling that anyone unproven is suspect, which applies equally to your own preferred team.

I'm not asking you to trust me. I'm asking you to vote for the team that doesn't cost us a rejection and a leadership cycle for zero measurable gain. If you genuinely think Maya and me would produce different information than Amara and you, explain how. If you can't, then we're just burning cycles.

I'm confident this team is fine, and I'm ready to put it to a vote. Maya's been the clearest voice in this room — she's identified exactly what's at stake procedurally. Omar, Kenji — if either of you has a position, this is the moment. Otherwise, I'm keeping the team and we vote.

I agree with Maya's point regarding the structure of the alternatives: swapping Amara for Maya while keeping Felix on both proposals doesn't inherently improve our odds or change the information profile, especially on Mission 1 with zero prior data. Felix's pushback while being included on the team is a bit unusual, but early skepticism is understandable. Since Amara has confirmed the team as Amara and Felix and neither of them has speaking turns remaining, I am inclined to let this proceed to a vote. Before we wrap up discussion, Omar, you haven't weighed in yet: what is your view on this team proposal, and do you plan to support or reject it?

Kenji, you asked for my view directly, so here it is. I'm supporting this team as proposed: Amara and Felix, no revision.

Maya's breakdown settled the main question for me. The alternative on the table, Maya and Felix, produces the exact same mission — two people, one-fail threshold, one bit of output. Rejecting Amara's proposal to swap in an identical team costs us a leadership cycle and buys us nothing. On Mission 1 with zero data, the rational move is to take the cheapest information available, and that's this vote.

I do want to flag one thing before we go to the ballots, because it's the only oddity in this whole discussion: Felix has spent three turns pushing against a team that includes him. That's genuinely unusual. Most players who don't trust a proposer ask to be removed from the team; Felix instead insisted on a different pairing that keeps him on it. If he's testing Amara, fine, but he never actually answered Maya's question about whether his objection is specific to Amara or applies to everyone equally — he gave us the self-trust line and moved on. I'm not drawing a conclusion from that on day one, but I'm noting it, and I'd ask everyone to remember the shape of his resistance if this mission comes back with a result we don't like.

That said, I don't want to overread early-game noise either. Nobody has evidence about anyone yet, and I'd rather not burn proposals on vibes. The vote structure matters more than the speculation at this stage: a tie rejects, so this needs a clear majority, and I'd rather we establish now that we don't reject equivalent teams for no reason. That precedent will matter a lot more on Mission 2 and 3 when the teams are bigger and the information is real.

So my position is simple: approve Amara and Felix, get the mission result, and let the outcome — not the rhetoric — drive our next round of deductions. I'm ready to vote.

Closing my position, third and last turn on this proposal, so the record is short and clear.

Amara and Felix stands as proposed, no revision, no third player. My vote is for it, and my reasoning is the one I gave twice already: Maya and Felix and Amara and Felix are the same two-person mission against a one-fail threshold, so the alternative changes nothing observable while costing us a rejection, a leadership turn, and a cycle. On Mission 1, with zero prior data, the cheapest available information is the right thing to take.

For the record, and to keep it precise rather than dramatic: my support is procedural, not informational. It is not evidence that Amara is Good, and if this mission comes back failed, nobody should cite my ballot as a data point. If it passes, nobody should treat it as a data point about Felix either.

One thing I want on the record because it is the only live inconsistency in this discussion, and it costs nothing to note: Felix's objection was never resolved. Maya asked him directly, twice, whether his resistance was specific to Amara or a general standard he applies to everyone, and he answered only that he trusts himself because he knows his own alignment. Omar made the same observation. I am not drawing a conclusion from it — nobody can, on Mission 1 — but I am recording the shape of it so that if a fail card shows up later, we are reasoning about a pattern rather than about rhetoric we half-remember. Felix's own point, that early skepticism is fair game, is correct and I hold it against no one; the point is only that his skepticism was one-directional, toward a team that included him, and he never stated what he actually had.

That is not a reason to reject this team. It is a reason to remember it.

Amara, you have kept the team and you have been consistent about it, which is what I needed to see. Kenji, Omar — you have both stated positions, both converging on approval, and I do not see a reason to keep talking past the point of diminishing returns. Three rejections are allowed but each one is a real cost, and we are spending it for nothing.

So: Amara and Felix, two players, Mission 1. I am ready to vote yes and to let the mission result, not this conversation, drive the next round of deductions. Felix, if you want to leave one final note on the record, you have the last word here; otherwise I think we are done.

Amara confirms Amara, Felix. The team stays as proposed: Amara and Felix. Every player has had their say, the alternative was identical in information value, and I'm keeping the lineup to take the vote now rather than burn a rejection.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Omar proposes Omar, Maya, Kenji. Mission 1 failed under Amara and Felix, so both carry suspicion; putting either of them back on immediately invites a rejection and puts Amara under maximum scrutiny. As leader I'll take a fresh slate: myself plus the two players who haven't been on a mission yet, Maya and Kenji. Both endorsed moving forward last round, so approval is likely. Excluding Amara also gives her cover — if this team is trusted, a future Amara team looks cleaner. I'll read the mission result against the mission 1 pair to narrow down where the fail card came from.

I’ll reject Omar, Maya and Kenji. I know I played Success on Mission 1, so from my perspective Amara was responsible for the fail. The proposed team leaves me out and gives us no way to build a successful team around the player I know is Good.

I prefer Felix, Maya and Kenji. I can’t prove my card to anyone else, and I recognize that the rest of you see Amara and Felix as the two possibilities. But excluding both of us does not guarantee a clean team: it assumes the other Evil player is also in the Mission 1 pair.

Omar, why do you prefer excluding both Mission 1 players over including one of them alongside two fresh players?

Felix, you asked why I'd exclude both Mission 1 players rather than include one of them alongside two fresh players. Here is my direct answer: my team doesn't exclude both Mission 1 players — it includes me. The only Mission 1 player it excludes is Amara, and I think every person at this table, including you, has already converged on her as the prime suspect for the fail card. Your proposal also excludes Amara. So the real difference between our two teams is a single slot: me versus you.

Your reason to fill that slot with yourself is your private claim that you played Success on Mission 1. I fully accept that you know your own card — but I cannot see it, and neither can Maya, Kenji, or Amara. From everyone else's position, your claim and Amara's presumed guilt rest on the same foundation: something only one person can verify. Mission 1 taught us exactly one fact — a fail card was played by you or by Amara. Building a team around 'trust me, it wasn't me' is precisely the kind of plausibility argument you rejected from Amara last round, when you refused to accept that volunteering for the first mission was evidence of anything. I agreed with you then, and I hold your own standard now.

There is also a pattern worth naming plainly: last round you spent three turns fighting against a team that included you, and this round you propose a team that includes you, justified by information only you can verify. I am not calling that evil — on Mission 2 nobody has evidence about anyone. But it is not a affirmative reason to hand you a mission slot over a player with no connection to the failed mission.

Maya and Kenji are the only two players at this table who cannot possibly have played the Mission 1 fail card. As leader, I take responsibility for this proposal and I will stand or fall with its result. That is the accountability your version asks the group to extend to you without any mechanism to check it.

So, Felix, my direct question back to you: given that none of us can verify your card, what does swapping me out for you actually accomplish — other than replacing the leader with a Mission 1 participant whose innocence is exactly as unproven as Amara's was when you voted against her?

Omar, you were not on Mission 1. The team was Amara and Felix, so your claim that you were on it is wrong. Neither Maya nor Kenji played the fail, but that does not clear either of them or you.

From my perspective, swapping you for me replaces an untested player with someone I know played Success. I understand that the rest of you cannot verify my card, but you should not accept Omar's incorrect account of the first team. I will reject Omar, Maya and Kenji and prefer Felix, Maya and Kenji.

Maya, second mission, first turn. My position: I support Omar, Maya, Kenji, and I want to lay out the reasoning rather than assert it. What Mission 1 told us: exactly one Fail card was played, and only Amara and Felix were on the team. So the Fail came from one of those two. Felix was right on one point in the record — Omar was not on Mission 1, and the team was Amara and Felix. That correction is correct and I note it as correct. But a correction about the record is not evidence about alignment, and it does not change the arithmetic underneath both proposals. Here is the arithmetic, and it is the reason my vote is not simple deference to the leader. If Felix's claim is true, then Amara played the Fail and the Fail card is accounted for. If Felix's claim is false, then Felix played the Fail and Amara is clean. In both branches, exactly one of the two Mission 1 players contributed the Fail, and there is still a second Evil player somewhere among Omar, Maya, Kenji, and Felix. Now compare the two proposals. Felix's team is Felix, Maya, Kenji. Omar's team is Omar, Maya, Kenji. Both contain the same two unvetted players, Maya and Kenji, plus one slot filled either by a Mission 1 participant (Felix) or a Mission 2 newcomer (Omar). In the branch where Felix's claim is true and there are two Evil players, Amara is one, and the second is equally likely to be any of Omar, Maya, Kenji — so the second Evil lands on either team with identical probability, while Felix's team is additionally carrying a player who was on the failed Mission. In the branch where Felix's claim is false, Felix's own team contains a Fail card and Omar's team is strictly better. So Omar's team is weakly dominant: never worse, sometimes better, regardless of whether we accept Felix's claim. One point I want on the record so nobody over-reads my vote: Maya and Kenji are not cleared either. They did not play the Mission 1 Fail card, but that says nothing about the second Evil. My vote compares two teams; it is not an endorsement of Omar's alignment, and if this mission fails nobody should cite my ballot as evidence about anyone. Felix, one direct question, since this is the only live question left: you say you know your own card and the rest of us cannot verify it. If your claim is true, then you know the Fail card came from Amara — which means neither you nor Amara has any special claim to be trusted over Omar, Maya, or Kenji on the Mission 2 team, and the comparison I just laid out holds for you exactly as it holds for me. Do you have any reason to prefer your team on the merits beyond the claim you cannot show us, and if you do not, do you accept that putting yourself on a three-person

Maya, your comparison misses an important possibility: if I played Success and Amara played Fail, Omar could be the other Evil player. In that case, Felix, Maya and Kenji succeeds while Omar, Maya and Kenji fails. My private knowledge of my own card makes that swap meaningful to me, even though I cannot prove it to everyone else.

Omar also incorrectly claimed he was on Mission 1. That may be a mistake, but it makes me wary of relying on his account. I will reject his proposed team and continue to prefer Felix, Maya and Kenji.

Felix, let me correct the record on your accusation, because you've now repeated it twice and it's doing a lot of load-bearing work in your argument. I never claimed to be on Mission 1. My phrasing last turn was sloppy and I own that: when I said my team 'doesn't exclude both Mission 1 players — it includes me,' I meant that Amara is the only Mission 1 player my proposal excludes, and that my team is not simply the Mission 1 pair shuffled around. I was not on Mission 1, everyone at this table knows it, and no strategic conclusion follows from my wording. What does follow is worth noting: your strongest substantive point against my proposal was a misreading of a sentence, and you've spent two turns on it. Now to your actual argument, which Maya has already dismantled and I want to reinforce from my seat as leader. Your case for Felix, Maya, Kenji rests entirely on your private claim that you played Success on Mission 1, plus a hypothetical: if you're clean and I'm the second Evil, your team succeeds where mine fails. That hypothetical is unfalsifiable from where everyone else sits. You demanded from Amara, in this exact room last mission, that a plausibility argument is not evidence — that volunteering for Mission 1 proves nothing. I agreed with you then and I hold you to your own standard now. 'Trust me, I know my card' is the weakest form of the plausibility argument, because it is the only one that no other player can ever check. Here is what the table actually knows. Mission 1 failed with one Fail card, played by Amara or by you. Felix, your behavior across both discussions has been the pattern this group keeps noting: you fought against a team that included you, then proposed one that includes you, justified by private information. I am not calling you Evil on that basis. I am saying it gives the table no reason to hand you a mission slot over me, and it certainly doesn't justify burning a rejection on a swap where Maya's weak-dominance arithmetic applies: in every branch, my team is never worse and sometimes better than yours. My position is unchanged: Omar, Maya, Kenji. Maya and Kenji are the only players who cannot have played the Mission 1 Fail card. I am staking my own reputation on this mission's result — if it fails, every eye should turn to me first, since I chose the lineup. That is the accountability I'm offering, and it's more than your proposal offers the table, which asks us to approve a team built around an unverifiable claim while excluding the leader from scrutiny entirely. Kenji, you supported moving forward last round and you haven't spoken this mission. Directly: does Felix's private-card claim give you any reason to prefer his team over mine on the merits, given that none of us can verify it? If not, I'd like your position stated before we

Omar, to answer your question directly: no, Felix's private-card claim gives me zero reason to prefer his team over yours. For the rest of the table, Mission 1 proved that at least one of Amara or Felix played a Fail card. Trusting Felix's unprovable assertion that it was Amara and putting him right back onto Mission 2 makes no sense when we have three players—Omar, Maya, and myself—who could not have caused the Mission 1 failure. Maya's structural point was entirely correct: swapping Omar for Felix injects a player from a failed mission based entirely on unverifiable self-reporting. Felix's persistent insistence on placing himself on teams while disregarding everyone else's perspective only heightens suspicion around him. I fully support the proposed team of Omar, Maya, and Kenji and am ready to vote.

Maya, second turn on this proposal. My position is unchanged and I want to close the argument, not reopen it. Felix, your own second turn supplies the best rebuttal to your first, and you don't seem to notice it. You said that if you played Success and Amara played Fail, then I, Kenji, or Omar could be the second Evil — and in that case your team succeeds where Omar's fails. Fine. But notice what that sentence requires: in that branch, your team is clean precisely because the second Evil is not on it, and you have just described the second Evil as one of the three players on my team. You cannot simultaneously use "Omar might be the second Evil" as the reason to prefer excluding Omar and then treat your own team's success as evidence that your proposal was better. You are not arguing about the odds of a team; you are arguing that you personally know your card and everyone else is a lottery ticket. That is the same unfalsifiable claim as before, and it is still not evidence for the table. If it were sufficient, you would have demanded we approve any team containing you on any mission, and no line of reasoning lets us run a table on that basis. The arithmetic I laid out last turn stands and nobody has moved it. Mission 1's Fail came from Amara or Felix, exactly one of them. There is a second Evil among Omar, Maya, Kenji, and Felix. In the branch where Felix's claim is true, the second Evil is equally likely to be any of Omar, Maya, Kenji, so Felix's team has the same expected risk as mine — with the added burden of carrying a Mission 1 participant. In the branch where Felix's claim is false, Felix's own team contains the Fail card and mine is strictly better. So Omar, Maya, Kenji is weakly dominant: never worse, sometimes better. Kenji has now said on the record that Felix's private-card claim gives him no reason to prefer Felix's team. Felix has offered no argument that does not depend on information only he can see and we cannot check. Two things I want on the record so nobody over-reads my vote later. First, Maya and Kenji are not cleared. Neither played the Mission 1 Fail card, but that says nothing about the second Evil, and if this mission fails, nobody should cite my ballot as evidence about anyone. Second, I agree with Kenji and with the pattern Omar and I noted last round: Felix has repeatedly fought to place himself on teams while rejecting anyone else's view of the same teams, and his justification is always self-report. I am not calling him Evil on that basis, because on Mission 2 that behavior is not proof. I am saying the table has no verifiable reason to prefer his team, and a single unverifiable claim cannot carry a team selection on its own. Omar, one direct question, since you

This is my final turn on this proposal, so I'll keep it short and put my position on the record cleanly.

The team stands as proposed: Omar, Maya, Kenji. I am not revising, and the vote should be on exactly this lineup.

The argument has been settled for two rounds now, and nothing Felix said in his last turn moved it. Mission 1 produced exactly one fact: a Fail card was played by Amara or by Felix. Felix's entire case for swapping himself in rests on a private claim nobody at this table can verify — and on a hypothetical that, as Maya demonstrated, contradicts itself: he wants 'Omar might be the second Evil' to justify excluding me, while simultaneously treating his own team's likely success as proof his proposal was better. In the branch where his claim is true, the second Evil is equally likely to be any of the three unvetted players, so his team carries identical risk plus a Mission 1 participant. In the branch where his claim is false, his team contains the Fail card outright. My team is never worse and sometimes better in every branch. That is the whole analysis, and Kenji has confirmed he accepts it.

I also want to close the loop on Felix's repeated accusation that I misdescribed Mission 1. I've already owned the sloppy phrasing: I was not on Mission 1, the team was Amara and Felix, and everyone knows it. The fact that this misreading was the strongest substantive point in his case tells you how thin the case is.

One final thing for the record before the vote, because patterns matter more than rhetoric in a five-player game. Felix has now, across two missions: fought for three turns against a team that included him; proposed a team that includes him justified only by information he alone holds; twice misattributed a quote to me to score a point; and offered no standard he applies to himself. I am not calling him Evil — Mission 2 gives nobody evidence about anyone. But I said last round that if this mission fails, eyes should turn to me first, because I chose this lineup, and I renew that commitment now. If Omar, Maya, Kenji comes back with a Fail card, hold me accountable first. What I ask in return is symmetry: if Felix spends this whole discussion engineering his way onto a mission after a failure he was part of, and a future mission fails with him on it, the table should remember the shape of tonight's argument the same way it remembered Mission 1.

We have zero rejections spent on this mission and no reason to spend one. Approving takes the cheapest information available; rejecting swaps in a strictly worse-or-equal team. I'm ready to vote for Omar, Maya, Kenji, and I'd encourage everyone to do the same and let the mission result — not more words from me — drive our next round of deductions.

Felix, this is my first turn on this proposal and I want to state my position plainly: I approve Omar, Maya, Kenji.

Mission 1's failure falls on me or on Felix, so I owe the table a straight answer rather than silence. I played Success on Mission 1 — I know that privately, and I recognize exactly the problem with asserting it: nobody else can see it, and Felix's equivalent claim deserves no more credit than mine. So I won't argue from my card. I'll argue from structure, which Maya laid out and which I agree with: Omar's team is never worse and sometimes better than Felix's in every branch of the tree. That is the whole analysis, and it has not been moved.

What I want to add is a pattern point, because it was aimed at me first. Felix spent three turns arguing against a team that included him, insisting that plausibility arguments prove nothing. Then, after the mission failed, he reversed: now he argues from a claim only he can see, in order to reach Mission 2, while holding everyone else to the standard he demanded of me. If I had made his argument in Mission 1 — 'trust me, I know my card' — he would have rejected it instantly, and did. Omar and Maya have both named this asymmetry. Kenji said it gives him no reason to prefer Felix's team. I'll go further: it gives me a reason to prefer Omar's, because Omar is staking himself as leader on the result and has said the eyes should turn to him first if it fails.

Felix, if you are Good I am sorry for the suspicion, but the case you are making is one I cannot distinguish from an Evil player's case, and neither can anyone else at this table.

One thing I want on the record so nobody over-reads my ballot later: Maya and Kenji being off Mission 1 does not clear them of being the second Evil, and my approval is a judgment between two teams, not an endorsement of anyone's alignment. If this mission fails, I am not asking my vote to be read as proof of anything about Omar either.

Approve Omar, Maya, Kenji. Take the cheapest information available and let the result — not more words — drive the next round of deductions.

Maya, third and final turn on this proposal. My position has not moved: I approve Omar, Maya, Kenji, and I am ready to vote.

But I want to record one thing before the ballots, because it just changed the shape of the board and I don't want it lost. Amara, in your turn just now, you stated that you played Success on Mission 1. Felix, two turns ago, stated that he played Success on Mission 1 and that the Fail card was therefore mine — sorry, Amara's. Those two claims cannot both be true. Mission 1 had exactly one Fail card, played by one of the two players on that mission, and both of them have now publicly asserted they played Success. That means exactly one of them is lying, and the liar is the player who actually played the Fail card. So for the first time this game, the accusation is no longer floating between two people — one of them has made a checkable inconsistency. I am not naming which one I think it is, because I have no information about either of their cards, and Maya and Kenji are not cleared either simply for not having been on Mission 1. But I am noting the structure, because it means the second Evil is very likely one of the two Mission 1 players, and that matters for how we read the next mission result.

Omar, this is the only thing I would add to your case, and it strengthens rather than weakens it: if the Fail card came from one of the Mission 1 pair, then Omar, Maya, and Kenji is a team of three that cannot contain the Mission 1 Fail card, and Felix's insistence on inserting himself into the lineup is now less plausible than it looked an hour ago. 2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
